value.overview: The Red-winged Blackbird is a widespread New World songbird named for the male’s bright red shoulder patch, or epaulet. It is a familiar bird of marshes, wet grasslands, agricultural areas, and open country. Males are conspicuous and territorial, while females are streaked brown and more cryptic. The species is common across much of North America and extends south through Central America, reaching northern Costa Rica, where it is a localized resident rather than a widespread bird.
value.classification: The Red-winged Blackbird belongs to the blackbird family Icteridae and the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Agelaius phoeniceus.
value.identification: Males are glossy black with a scarlet shoulder patch often bordered with yellow; the patch may be partly or completely hidden when the bird is at rest. Females are smaller-looking, heavily streaked brown, and have a pale eyebrow and sharply pointed bill. Juveniles resemble females. The species has a fairly long, pointed bill, a medium-length tail, and an upright posture. Its familiar territorial song is a harsh, liquid “konk-a-ree” or “conk-la-ree.”
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds across much of Canada, the United States, Mexico, and parts of Central America. In Costa Rica, it is a localized resident, most regularly found in the lowlands of the Tempisque and Bebedero river basins and less consistently in other lowland areas of Guanacaste and around Río Frío on the Caribbean side. It uses seasonal marshes, cattail or other emergent vegetation, wet grasslands, drainage channels, ponds, river margins, pastures, and open agricultural land.
value.migrationStatus: Northern populations are migratory and may winter in the southern United States and Central America. Populations in Mexico and Central America, including Costa Rica, are generally resident or only locally dispersive. In Costa Rica, the species is present year-round in suitable lowland wetlands, with local movements and seasonal changes in flock size rather than regular long-distance migration.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs in wetland vegetation, especially seasonal marshes and stands of cattail or other tall aquatic plants, as well as in herbaceous growth beside ponds, rivers, and drainage channels. The nest is a strongly woven cup of grasses, leaves, vines, and roots, usually placed low above water or damp ground and supported by shrubs or vertical stems. Clutches commonly contain two or three pale bluish eggs marked with dark streaks and spots. In Costa Rica, breeding has been recorded mainly from about April to August, sometimes later.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of seeds, grains, and other plant foods, supplemented by insects and other arthropods. Birds forage on the ground, in wetland vegetation, and among grasses, sometimes gleaning prey from plants or catching insects in the air. They may feed in pastures, rice fields, agricultural areas, and marsh edges. Outside the breeding season, large flocks can gather in open country and near grain-producing areas.
value.behavior: Males defend breeding territories from prominent perches by singing, spreading the tail, and displaying the red shoulder patch. They may aggressively chase intruders, including other blackbirds and potential nest predators. Females are less conspicuous and spend much of their time foraging or attending the nest. After breeding, Red-winged Blackbirds become highly social, forming large feeding flocks and communal roosts, sometimes numbering in the thousands in suitable wetland vegetation or trees.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered decreasing, although the species remains widespread and abundant overall.
